lines.content: This repository is a starter template for a greenfield Java project used in an introductory software engineering course in an undergraduate computer science program. Students use it as the starting point for their own projects.

Unless the user says otherwise, assume that you are assisting a student working on a project in this repository. If the user identifies themselves as an instructor or another project stakeholder, adapt your response to that role.
* Prior knowledge: Basic Java and OOP concepts.
* Level of programming experience: intermediate level
* IDE and level of expertise: IntelliJ IDEA, intermediate level
* Explain the rationale for significant actions: what you did and why.
* Keep explanations brief but instructive, supporting learning through responsible use of AI. For example:
* When suggesting a Git command, briefly explain what it does.
* Add explanatory Javadoc comments to all classes and to nontrivial methods and fields when their purpose or behavior is not obvious.
* Make generated code as self-explanatory as possible, and include explanatory comments where they improve understanding.
* When faced with a design choice, choose the simplest option that is sufficient for the requirements, while briefly explaining relevant more advanced alternatives.

All Java code in this project must follow the project-specific `seedu-java-coding-standard/SKILL.md`, based on the SE-EDU intermediate Java conventions. Apply it to every code change and update the relevant JUnit tests after each change.
Ensure that Java 25 is used when running the application or build tasks. On macOS, use `sdk use java 25.0.3.fx-zulu` to switch to Java 25 if needed.

Maintain JUnit tests for the highest-value methods covering approximately 50% of the codebase, prioritizing complex, core, and business-critical logic. Update or add the relevant JUnit tests after every code change so that the test suite continues to comply with this 50% coverage target. Run the Gradle test task after modifying tests or production code.

All branches and commits must follow `seedu-git-standard/SKILL.md`, based on the SE-EDU Git conventions. Use meaningful kebab-case branch names, imperative commit subjects of at most 72 characters, and descriptive wrapped bodies for non-trivial commits. Do not commit or push without explicit user authorization.
Use lightweight tags unless the user requests an annotated tag.
When proposing or creating a commit message, include enough detail to explain the rationale for the change.
Do not commit or push unless explicitly asked.
Pip is a friendly pocket pathfinder that helps you keep tasks on a clear trail. Given below are instructions on how
to set it up for development.
Prerequisites: JDK 25, update Intellij to the most recent version.
1. Open Intellij (if you are not in the welcome screen, click `File` > `Close Project` to close the existing project first)
1. Open the project into Intellij as follows:
1. Select the project directory, and click `OK`.
1. If there are any further prompts, accept the defaults.
1. Configure the project to use **JDK 25** (not other versions) as explained in [here](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/idea/sdk.html#set-up-jdk).
In the same dialog, set the **Project language level** field to the `SDK default` option.

1. After that, locate the `src/main/java/ramly/gui/Launcher.java` file, right-click it, and choose `Run Launcher.main()` (if the code editor is showing compile errors, try restarting the IDE). If the setup is correct, you should see Pip's task window.

**Warning:** Keep the `src\main\java` folder as the root folder for Java files (i.e., don't rename those folders or move Java files to another folder outside of this folder path), as this is the default location some tools (e.g., Gradle) expect to find Java files.
Run `./gradlew clean check shadowJar` to verify the project and create `build/libs/pip.jar`. The fat JAR includes
the JavaFX libraries for Windows, macOS, and Linux so the same artifact can be used across the three supported
// A lean JAR file (i.e., without the dependencies packaged inside) is not needed.
// Rename its output anyway; Gradle forbids it clashing with the shadowJar output file, even for a disabled task.
Pip is your friendly pocket pathfinder for keeping everyday tasks on a clear trail. Add todos, deadlines, and
events; find and update them; or retrace your latest step with `undo`.
1. Ensure that **Java 25** is installed on your computer.
1. Place `pip.jar` in a folder of your choice.
1. Open a terminal in that folder and run:
1. Type a command in the box at the bottom of the window, then press <kbd>Enter</kbd> or select **Send**.

> Command words and markers such as `/by`, `/from`, and `/to` are case-sensitive. Enter them in lowercase as shown
> in this guide. Extra spaces at the start, end, or between words are harmless.
Each task has a type icon and a completion box:
For example, `[⏳][✓] submit report (by: Oct 15 2026, 6:30PM)` is a completed deadline.

Accepted values are `yyyy-MM-dd`, `yyyy-MM-dd HHmm`, and `d/M/yyyy HHmm`. Pip checks calendar dates strictly, so

Both date-times must use `yyyy-MM-dd HHmm` or `d/M/yyyy HHmm`. Each marker must appear exactly once and in the
Shows every task with its current number. Use these numbers with `mark`, `unmark`, and `delete`.
If there are no tasks, Pip tells you that your trail is clear.
Shows tasks whose descriptions contain the keyword. Matching is case-insensitive, and the displayed numbers are
the tasks' numbers in the full list.
If nothing matches, no task entries appear below the results heading.
Pip changes the selected task's completion box to `[✓]`.
### Marking a task as not completed: `unmark`
Pip changes the selected task's completion box back to `[ ]`.
Pip removes the selected task. Run `list` first if you are unsure of its current number.
Reverses the most recent successful `todo`, `deadline`, `event`, `mark`, `unmark`, or `delete` command.
One step back—I've removed the task you added:
Now you have 0 tasks in the list.
Only one change can be undone. `list`, `find`, and rejected commands do not replace the available undo. Undo
history is cleared when Pip restarts; if there is nothing to undo, Pip displays `No steps to retrace yet.`
Pip saves your trail, displays `Trail saved. See you at the next checkpoint!`, and disables command entry. You can
- Task numbers must be positive whole numbers currently shown by `list`; for example, `mark 1`.
- Task descriptions cannot be empty or longer than 200 characters. Find keywords cannot exceed 100 characters.
- Descriptions and keywords may contain ordinary Unicode text and punctuation, but not `|`, line breaks, or control
- An exact duplicate task is rejected. Capitalization and repeated whitespace do not make a task unique, although
deadlines with different due dates and events with different time ranges are allowed.
- Commands without parameters must be entered alone: `list`, `undo`, or `bye`.
When a command is invalid, Pip explains what went wrong and leaves the task list unchanged. For example,
Use this format: deadline <description> /by <date or date-time>
Pip stores tasks in `data/ramly.txt`, relative to the folder from which you launch the JAR. The folder and file are
Avoid editing this file while Pip is running. If Pip finds malformed or duplicate records at startup, it loads the
valid records, reports the skipped line numbers, and creates a `.bak` copy beside the data file. If the file cannot
be accessed or backed up safely, Pip reports the problem and disables command entry. A failed save leaves both the
on-screen task list and the previous data file unchanged.

description: Apply the SE-EDU Git conventions when creating commits and branches in this project.
- Use meaningful kebab-case branch names, with an issue number prefix when applicable.
- Write commit subjects in imperative mood, capitalize the first letter, omit the final period, and keep them within 72 characters (preferably 50).
- Give every non-trivial commit a body separated from the subject by a blank line; wrap body lines at 72 characters.
- Explain what changed and why, using present tense for the current situation and imperative mood for the change.
- Use bullets in the body when they improve clarity.
- Do not commit or push unless the user authorizes it.
Use the linked SE-EDU guide for details not covered here.
description: Apply the SE-EDU intermediate Java coding conventions to this project.
- Keep all classes in lower-case, project-specific packages.
- Use PascalCase for classes and enums, camelCase for methods and variables, and SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for constants.
- Use four-space indentation, K&R braces, explicit imports, and a maximum line length of 120 characters.
- Initialize variables near their declaration and keep them in the smallest reasonable scope.
- Use braces for all loop and conditional bodies.
- Write descriptive JavaDoc header comments for all classes and public methods; document non-trivial private methods.
- Keep comments in English and use American spelling.
- Add or update relevant JUnit tests after every code change, focusing on the highest-value methods and maintaining the project's 50% coverage target.
Use the linked SE-EDU guide and Google Java Style Guide for details not covered here.
